dimension_grades.evidence: The author describes in detail spending five hours reading redis-om source code, writing a reproduction script, and even opening a GitHub issue before having any evidence — a fully detailed false lead.

The author explicitly states 'I had written them. I had reviewed my own PR... I had deployed them. And I had spent a day blaming a Redis library for my own event listener leak' — taking clear personal ownership.

The author quantifies wasted time explicitly: 'I had burned five hours chasing a library' and in the closing breakdown: '6 were spent on the Redis dead end, and maybe 3 were actual productive investigation.'

The tone is wry and self-deprecating without self-pity, e.g., 'I felt the specific kind of stupid that comes from not doing the obvious thing first' and 'the story gets good, and by "good" I mean "I wanted to crawl under my desk."'

The author shows the heap snapshot evidence (millions of small strings) before understanding what held them, and initially misreads them as a logging problem: 'I assumed we had a logging problem — that we were somehow buffering log output in memory.'

Clues build incrementally: Redis theory eliminated → heap snapshots taken → strings identified → retainer chain followed → RequestTracer found → _spans array discovered → but that's not the real cause → closure on metricsEmitter finally revealed.

The true root cause (the closure registered on metricsEmitter per request) is not revealed until the 'Thursday Afternoon' section, after sustained investigation through multiple wrong turns and partial discoveries.
Multiple emotional beats are present: 'My stomach dropped a little,' 'I wanted to crawl under my desk,' 'I have never been so happy to see a boring graph,' and 'felt the specific kind of stupid.'

Each takeaway names a specific behavior: checking deploy timelines first with a sticky note, grepping for '.on(' in PR reviews with a custom ESLint rule, taking heap snapshots in pairs with a bash script, and blocking self-reviewed PRs.
The author explicitly rejects generic advice: 'I'm not going to tell you to "always clean up your event listeners" or "monitor your memory usage." You know that. I knew that.'
Each takeaway connects to a specific narrative moment, e.g., 'If I'd done this on Wednesday morning, I would have eliminated the Redis library in thirty seconds instead of five hours.'
The author treats the reader as a peer: 'You know that. I knew that. Knowing it didn't stop me from writing the bug' — no lecturing, just sharing what changed for them personally.
There are exactly four code snippets (the alert, the RequestTracer class, the middleware with the leak, and the fix), each serving a distinct narrative purpose.
Critical lines are annotated with inline comments: '// <-- this included the full serialized request context', '// That's it. That's the whole method. // No cleanup.', and '// THIS. THIS RIGHT HERE.'
The leaking middleware code is shown in the 'Thursday Afternoon' section, and the fixed version is shown in 'The Fix' section, clearly contrasting the problematic pattern with the solution.
Before each snippet, prose directs attention: e.g., 'I opened the RequestTracer source file. It was 80 lines of code. I'd written every one of them. Here's the relevant section, stripped down.'

'I remember this because I got toothpaste on the screen trying to swipe it open' and 'still in boxers' and 'I came in Thursday with fresh eyes and a large coffee' provide concrete sensory/environmental details.
Real tool names are used throughout: PagerDuty, Datadog, Chrome DevTools, kubectl, ioredis, redis-om, pino, Express, ESLint, Kubernetes.
Key moments are dramatized as scenes: the toothpaste-on-phone alert, Priya's Slack message with quoted text, clicking through the retainer chain in DevTools, and staring at the three lines of code.
